content: Depigmentation refers to the process of skin lightening or the loss of pigment in the skin. This condition can arise due to various local or systemic factors. The loss of pigment may be partial, such as in cases of skin injury, or complete, as seen in vitiligo. It can also be temporary, as in tinea versicolor, or permanent, as in albinism. Among these, vitiligo is the most common condition associated with depigmentation. Individuals with vitiligo who choose to fully depigment their skin often use a topical cream containing the organic compound monobenzone to remove the remaining pigment. A well-known brand of this medication is Benoquin, which contains 20% monobenzone and is manufactured by ICN. Recently, there has been an increase in the use of lower-concentration, self-compounded monobenzone creams by individuals without vitiligo, aiming to achieve an even skin tone. Another chemical used for skin lightening is mequinol, which is applied over an extended period. Both monobenzone and mequinol can produce significant skin whitening, but their mechanisms and effects differ. For persistent pigmented lesions, treatments such as Q-switched ruby lasers, cryotherapy, or trichloroacetic acid (TCA) peels may be employed to maintain pigment-free skin. Mequinol typically leaves the skin looking very pale, but tanning remains possible. In contrast, monobenzone, when applied topically, permanently removes pigment, necessitating strict lifelong sun protection. Individuals without vitiligo who use monobenzone often do so because standard skin-lightening products containing hydroquinone or other agents are ineffective for their needs, or due to the cost and potency of active ingredients in alternative treatments. However, monobenzone is not recommended for skin conditions other than vitiligo.
